name: Alva
title: Chieftain in Edom
summary: Alva is one of the chiefs mentioned in the list of Edomite tribal princes in Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1. The name appears exclusively in this chief list and not among the named descendants of Esau in the preceding genealogies, which has led scholars to discuss whether Alva refers to an individual, a clan, or a geographical district. The entry testifies to the early organization of tribal society in the Edom region and to the Bible's interest in documenting also the collateral lines in Abraham's family.

keyEvents.title: Listed among the chieftains of Edom
keyEvents.description: Alva is mentioned in the list of tribal princes in Esau's land, Edom. The list enumerates the chieftains by their names and associated regions, providing a picture of clan-based governance in the area.

keyEvents.title: Repeated in the genealogies of Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Alva is also included in 1 Chronicles' summary of the chieftains of Edom, confirming that this tradition was preserved and regarded as important in Israelite historiography.

versions.summary: Alva was one of the chieftains (tribal princes) descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. He is mentioned in the genealogies in Genesis 1 and 1 Chronicles as one of the chieftains of Edom. His role illustrates the spread of Esau's descendants in the region of Edom.
versions.title: Chieftain from Esau's line

The father should be set to 'Eliphaz'.; [major] Alva had several brothers through Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zepho/Zephi, Gatam and Kenaz (as well as Amalek through Timna). These should be listed as siblings.; [minor] The role 'leader' is clear, but 'chief' or 'tribal prince' would have been more precise and descriptive of Alva's role as one of the chiefs of Edom.; [major] In Gen 36:11, the sons of Eliphaz are given as Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz. It is possible that Alva in verse 40 refers to a clan or chieftain title rather than a direct son mentioned in verse 11. versions.summary: Alva was one of the chiefs (tribal princes) in Edom, connected to Esau's descendants. He is mentioned in the list of Edomite chiefs in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. The name may refer to a clan or an area in Edom just as much as to an individual. His role illustrates the spread and organization of Esau's descendants in the Edom region southeast of the Dead Sea.
versions.title: Chief in Edom from Esau's line

footnotes.text: The name Alva (Hebrew: עַלְוָה, 'Alvah') may mean 'exalted' or 'injustice'. In some Hebrew manuscripts and translations, the variant Alvan (עַלְוָן) appears. Scholars debate whether the name refers to an individual, a clan, or a geographical area in Edom.

The list of Edomite chiefs in Gen 36:40–43 is considered by many scholars to represent geographic and clan-based divisions rather than individual leaders. These names may have served as designations for territories or clans within the Edomite tribal community.

The Edom region, southeast of the Dead Sea along the trade route to Arabia, was strategically and economically important in the Bronze Age. Archaeological excavations at sites such as Buseira and Tawilan have uncovered traces of early settlement and organized communities that align with biblical descriptions of Edomite chiefs.

There is an important distinction between the different lists in Gen 36. Verses 10–14 describe Esau's sons and grandsons, while verses 40–43 list chiefs by names that may also be understood as territories. Alva appears only in the latter list, which may indicate that it reflects a different tradition or a later political-geographic organization of Edom.

In rabbinic tradition, Edom and its chiefs were often interpreted typologically as representatives of worldly power in contrast to Israel's spiritual calling. The chiefs of Edom were seen as examples showing that Esau's line gained worldly influence early on, in accordance with the blessing in Gen 27:39–40.
